title: Lecture 1: Markov Chains
text:
Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space and let
\[
X_0,X_1,X_2,\ldots
\]
be random variables taking values in a countable set \(S\). We give \(S\) the discrete \(\sigma\)-field \(2^S\).

title: Lecture 1: Markov Chains
text:
1. Definition of a Markov chain
Definition. The sequence \(\{X_n\}_{n\geq 0}\) is called a Markov chain if, for every \(n\geq 0\) and every \(i_0,\ldots,i_n,j\in S\) such that the conditioning event has positive probability,
\[
\mathbb P
\left(
X_{n+1}=j
\mid
X_n=i_n,X_{n-1}=i_{n-1},\ldots,X_0=i_0
\right)
=
\mathbb P
\left(
X_{n+1}=j
\mid
X_n=i_n
\right).
\tag{1}
\]
Thus, once the present state \(X_n\) is specified, the conditional distribution of \(X_{n+1}\) does not depend on the values taken by the chain before time \(n\).
If
\[
\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i)
\]
does not depend on \(n\), then the chain is called time-homogeneous. In that case we write
\[
p(i,j)
=
\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i).
\tag{2}
\]
The number \(p(i,j)\) is called the transition probability from \(i\) to \(j\).
For each fixed \(i\in S\),
\[
p(i,j)\geq 0
\]
for every \(j\in S\), and
\[
\sum_{j\in S}p(i,j)=1.
\tag{3}
\]
Throughout these notes, unless explicitly stated otherwise, our Markov chains will be time-homogeneous.

A small point about conditioning
When we write a conditional probability such as
\[
\mathbb P
\left(
X_{n+1}=j
\mid
X_n=i_n,\ldots,X_0=i_0
\right),
\]
we are assuming that
\[
\mathbb P(X_n=i_n,\ldots,X_0=i_0)>0.
\]
The conditional-expectation formulation below removes the need to keep repeating this qualification, since conditional expectations are defined up to almost-sure equality.

title: Lecture 1: Markov Chains
text:
2. Examples

Example 1: An i.i.d. sequence
Let \(X_0,X_1,\ldots\) be i.i.d. random variables taking values in \(S\).
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb P
\left(
X_{n+1}=j
\mid
X_n=i_n,\ldots,X_0=i_0
\right)\\
&\qquad =
\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j)
\end{aligned}
\]
by independence. Similarly,
\[
\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i_n)
=
\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j).
\]
Hence
\[
\mathbb P
\left(
X_{n+1}=j
\mid
X_n=i_n,\ldots,X_0=i_0
\right)
=
\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i_n),
\]
so \(\{X_n\}\) is a Markov chain.
Since the random variables are identically distributed,
\[
\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j)
=
\mathbb P(X_0=j)
\]
for every \(n\). Therefore the transition probabilities do not depend on time, and the chain is time-homogeneous.
In fact,
\[
p(i,j)=\mathbb P(X_0=j),
\]
so the transition probability does not depend on \(i\) either.
Thus an i.i.d. sequence is a particularly simple Markov chain: the next state does not even depend on the present one.


Example 2: Random walk on a countable group
Let \(G\) be a countable group. For simplicity of notation, write the group operation additively.
Let
\[
X_1,X_2,\ldots
\]
be i.i.d. \(G\)-valued random variables and define
\[
S_0=0,
\qquad
S_m=\sum_{r=1}^{m}X_r.
\tag{4}
\]
Then
\[
S_n=S_{n-1}+X_n.
\]
We claim that \(\{S_n\}_{n\geq 0}\) is a Markov chain.
Suppose
\[
S_{n-1}=i_{n-1},\ldots,S_0=i_0.
\]
Then
\[
S_n=j
\]
if and only if
\[
X_n=j-i_{n-1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb P
\left(
S_n=j
\mid
S_{n-1}=i_{n-1},\ldots,S_0=i_0
\right)\\
&\qquad =
\mathbb P
\left(
X_n=j-i_{n-1}
\mid
S_{n-1}=i_{n-1},\ldots,S_0=i_0
\right).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
\]
Now
\[
S_0,S_1,\ldots,S_{n-1}
\]
are all functions of
\[
X_1,\ldots,X_{n-1}.
\]
Hence
\[
\sigma(S_0,\ldots,S_{n-1})
\subseteq
\sigma(X_1,\ldots,X_{n-1}).
\]
But \(X_n\) is independent of
\[
\sigma(X_1,\ldots,X_{n-1}),
\]
and therefore it is independent of
\[
\sigma(S_0,\ldots,S_{n-1}).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb P
\left(
X_n=j-i_{n-1}
\mid
S_{n-1}=i_{n-1},\ldots,S_0=i_0
\right)\\
&\qquad =
\mathbb P(X_n=j-i_{n-1}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since the \(X_n\) are identically distributed,
\[
\mathbb P(X_n=j-i)
=
\mathbb P(X_1=j-i),
\]
which does not depend on \(n\).
Thus \(\{S_n\}\) is a time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition probabilities
\[
p(i,j)
=
\mathbb P(X_1=j-i).
\tag{6}
\]
For a non-abelian group the same argument works with the group operation written multiplicatively.

title: Lecture 1: Markov Chains
section: 3. Conditional-expectation formulation of the Markov property
text:
3. Conditional-expectation formulation of the Markov property
The Markov property can be written more cleanly using conditional expectation.
Let
\[
\mathcal F_n^X
=
\sigma(X_0,X_1,\ldots,X_n).
\]
Lemma. Let \(\{X_n\}_{n\geq0}\) be a Markov chain with countable state space \(S\). If \(f:S\to[0,\infty]\) is Borel measurable, then
\[
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)
\right)
=
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
X_n
\right)
\quad\text{a.s.}
\tag{7}
\]
If \(f(X_{n+1})\) is integrable, then the same conclusion holds for real-valued \(f\).

Proof
We prove this in the same order in which measurable functions are built: first indicators, then simple functions, and finally general nonnegative measurable functions.

Step 1: Indicator functions
Fix \(j\in S\) and take
\[
f(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{j\}}(x).
\]
Then
\[
f(X_{n+1})
=
\mathbf 1_{\{X_{n+1}=j\}}.
\]
For every \(i_0,\ldots,i_n\in S\) for which
\[
\mathbb P(X_0=i_0,\ldots,X_n=i_n)>0,
\]
we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E
\left(
\mathbf 1_{\{X_{n+1}=j\}}
\mid
X_0=i_0,\ldots,X_n=i_n
\right)\\
&\qquad =
\mathbb P
\left(
X_{n+1}=j
\mid
X_0=i_0,\ldots,X_n=i_n
\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
By the Markov property,
\[
\mathbb P
\left(
X_{n+1}=j
\mid
X_0=i_0,\ldots,X_n=i_n
\right)
=
\mathbb P
\left(
X_{n+1}=j
\mid
X_n=i_n
\right).
\]
Again using the relation between indicators and conditional probabilities,
\[
\mathbb P
\left(
X_{n+1}=j
\mid
X_n=i_n
\right)
=
\mathbb E
\left(
\mathbf 1_{\{X_{n+1}=j\}}
\mid
X_n=i_n
\right).
\]
Hence
\[
\mathbb E
\left(
\mathbf 1_{\{X_{n+1}=j\}}
\mid
\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)
\right)
=
\mathbb E
\left(
\mathbf 1_{\{X_{n+1}=j\}}
\mid
X_n
\right)
\quad\text{a.s.}
\tag{8}
\]
The same conclusion holds for the indicator of an arbitrary subset \(A\subseteq S\).
Indeed, because \(S\) is countable,
\[
\mathbf 1_{\{X_{n+1}\in A\}}
=
\sum_{j\in A}\mathbf 1_{\{X_{n+1}=j\}},
\]
where the sum is understood as the increasing limit of the finite partial sums. Equivalently, one may simply sum the conditional probabilities over \(j\in A\). Thus
\[
\mathbb E
\left(
\mathbf 1_{\{X_{n+1}\in A\}}
\mid
\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)
\right)
=
\mathbb E
\left(
\mathbf 1_{\{X_{n+1}\in A\}}
\mid
X_n
\right).
\tag{9}
\]


Step 2: Simple functions
Now let \(f\) be a nonnegative simple function on \(S\). Write
\[
f
=
\sum_{r=1}^{m}a_r\mathbf 1_{A_r},
\qquad
a_r\geq0,
\]
where \(A_r\subseteq S\).
Then
\[
f(X_{n+1})
=
\sum_{r=1}^{m}
a_r
\mathbf 1_{\{X_{n+1}\in A_r\}}.
\]
Using linearity of conditional expectation and (9),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)
\right)\\
&\qquad =
\sum_{r=1}^{m}
a_r
\mathbb E
\left(
\mathbf 1_{\{X_{n+1}\in A_r\}}
\mid
\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)
\right)\\
&\qquad =
\sum_{r=1}^{m}
a_r
\mathbb E
\left(
\mathbf 1_{\{X_{n+1}\in A_r\}}
\mid
X_n
\right)\\
&\qquad =
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
X_n
\right).
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]
Thus the result is true for every nonnegative simple function.


Step 3: Nonnegative Borel functions
Let now
\[
f:S\to[0,\infty]
\]
be Borel measurable.
There exists a sequence of nonnegative simple functions \(f_m\) such that
\[
f_m\uparrow f
\]
pointwise.
Therefore
\[
f_m(X_{n+1})
\uparrow
f(X_{n+1}).
\]
For each \(m\), Step 2 gives
\[
\mathbb E
\left(
f_m(X_{n+1})
\mid
\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)
\right)
=
\mathbb E
\left(
f_m(X_{n+1})
\mid
X_n
\right).
\tag{11}
\]
Conditional expectation respects increasing limits: if \(Y_m\uparrow Y\) with all \(Y_m\geq0\), then
\[
\mathbb E(Y_m\mid\mathcal G)
\uparrow
\mathbb E(Y\mid\mathcal G)
\quad\text{a.s.}
\]
Hence, letting \(m\to\infty\) in (11),
\[
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)
\right)
=
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
X_n
\right).
\]
This proves (7) for every nonnegative Borel function \(f\).
Finally, if \(f(X_{n+1})\) is integrable, write
\[
f=f^+-f^-.
\]
Both \(f^+\) and \(f^-\) are nonnegative, so applying the result to them separately and subtracting gives
\[
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)
\right)
=
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
X_n
\right).
\]
This completes the proof.



Remark: the converse
The converse is immediate once the statement is assumed for every Borel function \(f\).
Suppose
\[
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)
\right)
=
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
X_n
\right)
\]
for every bounded Borel \(f\).
Take
\[
f(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{j\}}(x).
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb P
\left(
X_{n+1}=j
\mid
\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)
\right)\\
&\qquad =
\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n),
\end{aligned}
\]
which is precisely the Markov property.
Notice that equality only for the particular choice \(f(x)=x\) would not be enough: equality of conditional means does not in general determine equality of conditional distributions. The statement for all indicator functions, or equivalently all bounded Borel functions, does.

title: Lecture 1: Markov Chains
section: 4. We need not condition on consecutive past times
text:
4. We need not condition on consecutive past times
A useful consequence of the lemma is that the earlier times appearing in the conditioning need not be consecutive.
Let
\[
0\leq r_1<r_2<\cdots<r_k<n
\]
and consider
\[
\mathcal G
=
\sigma(X_{r_1},\ldots,X_{r_k},X_n).
\]
Then
\[
\mathcal G
\subseteq
\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n).
\]
Let \(f:S\to[0,\infty]\) be Borel measurable. By the tower property,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
\mathcal G
\right)\\
&\qquad =
\mathbb E
\left[
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)
\right)
\Bigm|
\mathcal G
\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
By the lemma,
\[
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)
\right)
=
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
X_n
\right).
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
\mathcal G
\right)\\
&\qquad =
\mathbb E
\left[
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
X_n
\right)
\Bigm|
\mathcal G
\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
But
\[
\mathbb E(f(X_{n+1})\mid X_n)
\]
is \(\sigma(X_n)\)-measurable, and
\[
\sigma(X_n)\subseteq\mathcal G.
\]
Hence
\[
\mathbb E
\left[
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
X_n
\right)
\Bigm|
\mathcal G
\right]
=
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
X_n
\right).
\]
Thus
\[
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
X_{r_1},\ldots,X_{r_k},X_n
\right)
=
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
X_n
\right).
\tag{12}
\]
Taking
\[
f(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{j\}}(x)
\]
gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb P
\left(
X_{n+1}=j
\mid
X_n=i,\,
X_{r_1}=i_1,\ldots,X_{r_k}=i_k
\right)\\
&\qquad =
\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i),
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
\]
whenever the conditioning event has positive probability.
So in the Markov property, the past variables we retain need not occur at consecutive times.

title: Lecture 1: Markov Chains
text:
Exercise 1
Let \(0\leq k<n+1\).
First prove that
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb P
\left(
X_{n+1}=j
\mid
X_k=i_k,X_{k-1}=i_{k-1},\ldots,X_0=i_0
\right)\\
&\qquad =
\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_k=i_k).
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]
Thus, even when \(X_{n+1}\) is several time-steps ahead of \(X_k\), the entire history up to time \(k\) can be replaced by the single variable \(X_k\).
Then prove the corresponding conditional-expectation statement:
\[
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_k)
\right)
=
\mathbb E
\left(
f(X_{n+1})
\mid
X_k
\right)
\tag{15}
\]
for every nonnegative Borel \(f\), and hence for every integrable \(f\).
A natural first step is to prove (14) by induction on \(n+1-k\).
The first correct solution posted in the comments, with Exercise 1 clearly marked, will be cited and added to the notes.

title: Lecture 1: Markov Chains
section: 5. Transition probabilities as an abstract object
text:
5. Transition probabilities as an abstract object
We now forget, for the moment, about an already existing Markov chain and start only with a possible transition rule.
Definition. A function
\[
p:S\times S\longrightarrow\mathbb R
\]
is called a transition probability function if
\[
p(i,j)\geq0
\]
for all \(i,j\in S\), and
\[
\sum_{j\in S}p(i,j)=1
\]
for every \(i\in S\).
Thus, for each fixed \(i\), the numbers
\[
\{p(i,j):j\in S\}
\]
form a probability distribution on \(S\).
The transition probabilities of every time-homogeneous Markov chain satisfy these conditions.
The converse question is now natural:

Given a countable state space \(S\) and a transition probability function \(p\), can we construct a Markov chain having exactly these transition probabilities?

The answer is yes.

title: Lecture 1: Markov Chains
section: 6. Construction of a Markov chain from its transition probabilities
text:
6. Construction of a Markov chain from its transition probabilities
Let \(S\) be countable and let
\[
p:S\times S\to[0,1]
\]
be a transition probability function.
Choose a probability measure \(\mu\) on \(S\); this will be the distribution of the initial state.
For the construction it is not necessary that every point have positive \(\mu\)-probability. However, if we want a measure on \(S\) having no nonempty null set, we may choose \(\mu\) so that
\[
\mu(i)>0
\]
for every \(i\in S\).
For example, if \(S\) is finite, we may take the discrete uniform distribution
\[
\mu(i)=\frac1{|S|}.
\]
If
\[
S=\{s_1,s_2,\ldots\},
\]
we may take
\[
\mu(s_r)=\frac1{2^r},
\qquad r\geq1,
\]
since
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac1{2^r}=1.
\]
Now take the path space
\[
\Omega=S^{\mathbb N_0}.
\]
Thus an element of \(\Omega\) is an infinite sequence
\[
\omega=(\omega_0,\omega_1,\omega_2,\ldots).
\]
For \(n\geq0\), define the coordinate projection
\[
X_n(\omega)=\omega_n.
\tag{16}
\]
We want to put a probability measure on \(\Omega\) such that these coordinate projections form a Markov chain with transition probability \(p\).

Exact cylinder sets
For \(i_0,\ldots,i_n\in S\), define
\[
A_{i_0,\ldots,i_n}
=
\{
\omega\in\Omega:
\omega_0=i_0,\ldots,\omega_n=i_n
\}.
\tag{17}
\]
Thus \(A_{i_0,\ldots,i_n}\) is the event that the first \(n+1\) coordinates of the path are exactly
\[
i_0,i_1,\ldots,i_n.
\]
These sets have the useful property already visible from their definition:
if
\[
A_{i_0,\ldots,i_n}
\quad\text{and}\quad
A_{j_0,\ldots,j_m}
\]
are two such cylinder sets, then either they are disjoint, or the longer specification extends the shorter one, in which case one cylinder is contained in the other.
For example,
\[
A_{1,2,3,4}\subseteq A_{1,2},
\]
whereas
\[
A_{1,2,3}
\cap
A_{1,5}
=
\varnothing.
\]
On an exact cylinder we prescribe
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(A_{i_0,\ldots,i_n})
=
\mu(i_0)
p(i_0,i_1)
p(i_1,i_2)
\cdots
p(i_{n-1},i_n).
}
\tag{18}
\]
This is the only reasonable formula: start at \(i_0\) with probability \(\mu(i_0)\), then make the successive transitions
\[
i_0\to i_1\to\cdots\to i_n.
\]
The first thing to check is consistency.
If we specify the path only up to \(i_n\), then summing over all possibilities for the next state must return the same probability. Indeed,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j\in S}
\mathbb P(A_{i_0,\ldots,i_n,j})
&=
\sum_{j\in S}
\mu(i_0)
p(i_0,i_1)\cdots p(i_{n-1},i_n)p(i_n,j)\\
&=
\mu(i_0)
p(i_0,i_1)\cdots p(i_{n-1},i_n)
\sum_{j\in S}p(i_n,j)\\
&=
\mu(i_0)
p(i_0,i_1)\cdots p(i_{n-1},i_n)\\
&=
\mathbb P(A_{i_0,\ldots,i_n}).
\end{aligned}
\tag{19}
\]
The equality in the third line follows from
\[
\sum_{j\in S}p(i_n,j)=1.
\]
More generally, summing over any finite number of unspecified future coordinates gives back the probability of the shorter cylinder.


The cylinder \(\sigma\)-field
Let \(\mathcal F\) be the \(\sigma\)-field on \(S^{\mathbb N_0}\) generated by the finite-coordinate cylinder sets.
For a completely formal use of the extension theorem, it is convenient to allow a cylinder to specify an arbitrary set of possible values of the first finitely many coordinates.
For \(B\subseteq S^{n+1}\), write
\[
C_n(B)
=
\{
\omega\in\Omega:
(\omega_0,\ldots,\omega_n)\in B
\}.
\tag{20}
\]
Since \(S\) is countable, \(S^{n+1}\) is countable. Define
\[
\mu_n(B)
=
\sum_{(i_0,\ldots,i_n)\in B}
\mu(i_0)
p(i_0,i_1)\cdots p(i_{n-1},i_n).
\tag{21}
\]
Then \(\mu_n\) is a probability measure on \(S^{n+1}\).
Equation (19) says precisely that these finite-dimensional probability measures are consistent:
\[
\mu_{n+1}(B\times S)=\mu_n(B).
\tag{22}
\]
Thus the probability assigned to a cylinder does not depend on whether we regard it as a condition on the first \(n+1\) coordinates or as the same condition with some later coordinates left unrestricted.
The collection of finite-coordinate cylinders is an algebra, and the consistent probabilities above define the usual cylinder premeasure on it. By the Carathéodory extension theorem in its cylinder-set form, this premeasure extends uniquely to a probability measure
\[
\mathbb P
\]
on
\[
(\Omega,\mathcal F).
\]
Hence we have constructed a genuine probability space carrying the coordinate random variables
\[
X_n(\omega)=\omega_n.
\]

title: Lecture 1: Markov Chains
text:
Exercise 2
Prove that the coordinate projections
\[
X_n(\omega)=\omega_n
\]
form a time-homogeneous Markov chain on \(S\) with transition probability function \(p\).
In particular, show that whenever
\[
\mathbb P
\left(
X_0=i_0,\ldots,X_n=i_n
\right)>0,
\]
we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb P
\left(
X_{n+1}=j
\mid
X_0=i_0,\ldots,X_n=i_n
\right)\\
&\qquad =
p(i_n,j),
\end{aligned}
\tag{23}
\]
and therefore
\[
\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i)=p(i,j).
\tag{24}
\]
The first correct solution posted in the comments, with Exercise 2 clearly marked, will be cited and added to the notes.
Consequently, every transition probability function on a countable state space can be realised by a time-homogeneous Markov chain.

title: Stochastic Processes
text:
This blog willl develop an introductory Graduate Course on Stochastic Processes,with the contents ranging from Discrete Time Homogenous Markov Chains with emphasis on Finite State Space.This will be folloed by a treatment of Poisson Processes and we will end with an introduction to Martingales and Brownian Motion.
Each Blog will contain some small excercises that may include some small generalisations,prompting to finish some specific steps of a proof or working out an example.
If you intend to submit a solution kindly type it in the comment box with reference to the excercise number.The first correct and complete solution will be added to the notes citing the solution provider.
The principal reference is:
